Unthankful
ŭn-thăngk'fəl
adj. (ungrateful; not returning thanks for benefits received)
English un-, not, with thankful, from thank, akin to think — gratitude is a work of the mind before it is a word of the mouth. The Greek acharistos is the negative of charis, grace: the man who does not acknowledge a favour.

Biblical Definition

Ingratitude is not a small fault in Scripture; it stands at the head of the descent in Romans and in the middle of the marks of the last days. “For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2Ti 3:2). Romans traces the whole ruin of the heathen mind back to this point: “Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom 1:21). The darkening of the mind followed the failure of thanks. Most striking of all is where the Lord Jesus places the word: “But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil” (Luk 6:35). God's own kindness reaches the ungrateful, and that is offered as the pattern for a Christian's dealings with men who will never say thank you. Against all of it stands the plain command: “In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you” (1Th 5:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines unthankful as ungrateful; not thankful; not making acknowledgments for good received; and unthankfulness as neglect or omission of acknowledgment for favors.

expand to see more

UNTHANKFUL, a. Ungrateful; not thankful; not making acknowledgments for good received.

He is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Luke vi.

UNTHANKFULLY, adv. Without thanks; ungratefully.

UNTHANKFULNESS, n. Neglect or omission of acknowledgment for good received; ingratitude.

Key Scripture

2Ti 3:2 — "For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,"

Rom 1:21 — "Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened."

Luk 6:35 — "But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil."

1Th 5:18 — "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you."

Modern Corruption

Gratitude has been reduced to a private discipline that improves the one who practises it, when Romans 1:21 presents thanklessness as the hinge on which a mind turns dark.

expand to see more

Thankfulness is now widely recommended, and recommended for the wrong reason. It is taught as a practice that benefits the practitioner — keep a list of good things, notice them, and your outlook improves. Everything in that account is true except what matters: it has no object. Thanks in Scripture is always thanks to someone, and its absence is not a mood but a refusal to name a Giver. That is exactly Paul's argument. Men knew God, glorified Him not as God, neither were thankful, and from that point the reasoning went vain and the heart went dark. Ingratitude is therefore not the last symptom of unbelief but one of its first causes, and a discipline of noticing blessings while declining to name the One who sent them is not obedience to 1 Thessalonians 5:18 but a more comfortable way of doing the thing Romans 1 describes.

The second corruption is inside the church, and it is the assumption that thanks is owed only when the providence is pleasant. The apostle writes in every thing, which is not the same as for every thing; a Christian is not commanded to call evil good, but he is commanded to give thanks in the middle of it, because the God who governs the loss is the same God who gave the mercies. Where that is lost the household becomes a place of complaint, and complaint is contagious in a way gratitude has to be taught. The Lord's own example in Luke 6:35 sets the standard higher still: God is kind unto the unthankful. A man who will only be generous to those who acknowledge it has not yet learned how he was treated himself, for the whole of his salvation was given to him while he was still ungrateful.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek acharistos (G884), unthankful, from a-, not, and charis, grace or favour; set against eucharisteo (G2168), to give thanks.

expand to see more

Greek acharistos (G884) — ungrateful, unthankful; used twice, of the last days and of those to whom God is nonetheless kind; 2 Timothy 3:2, Luke 6:35.

Greek eucharisteo (G2168) — to give thanks, to be grateful; the verb over the bread at the Supper; Luke 22:19, 1 Thessalonians 5:18.

Greek charis (G5485) — grace, favour; the root the unthankful man denies by not acknowledging it.

Hebrew yadah (H3034) — to give thanks, literally to cast out the hand; the standing word of the Psalter's praise; Psalm 107:1.

Hebrew todah (H8426) — thanksgiving, a thank offering; sacrifice and gratitude joined in one word; Psalm 50:14.

Usage

"“Neither were thankful” — the hinge on which Romans 1 turns toward darkness."

"“He is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil” — the pattern for dealing with men who never say thank you."

"“In every thing give thanks” — in every thing, which is not the same as for every thing."
